AI read · Citrini · today's macro tape

The setup is stressed price action with a quiet volatility market. The Crash Index reads 6/10, the regime score is 68 with 4 risk-off signals aligned, and the macro regime is CONTRACTION at 70% confidence. Yet the VIX spike detector sits at tier 1/4 with a 50% probability and no backwardation. Small caps fell -5.1% and the Nasdaq 100 fell -6.3% over five days, so the damage is real and the fear premium is still thin.

That gap shapes your positioning. The contrarian score of 100 tells you sellers are exhausted, but the contraction regime and the lit credit and yen confluences say the exit is not clean yet. Hold reduced gross exposure and favor hedges that are cheap while the VIX stays unstressed. Add to longs in stages only after the curve confirms a spike, because capitulation lows usually print with backwardation, and you do not have it today.

The main risk is a slow grind lower where options never reprice and the credit and yen signals keep building. The flip is a VIX move into backwardation with the Crash Index easing from 6. That combination turns the contrarian score from a setup into an entry.

Macro Regime — where are we structurally
AI read · macro regime

The regime reads CONTRACTION at 70% confidence, and the regime score of 68 sits in TRANSITION with a risk-off bias from 4 aligned signals. Contraction means growth and credit conditions are tightening, and that favors quality balance sheets, shorter duration risk and smaller position sizes over high-beta growth.

The yield curve pair (t10y2y) shifting its correlation from -0.60 to +0.35 supports the view that rates are repricing the growth outlook. Keep the contrarian score of 100 on a watchlist rather than acting on it, because capitulation buying works best once the regime score leaves transition.

Raise risk only when the regime label moves out of CONTRACTION or the confidence level drops well below 70%.

Cross-asset divergence radar — Cross-asset divergence watch
AI read · divergences in plain English

Divergence means two assets that normally move together are now moving apart. Correlation drift measures how much that link has changed, from the old reading to the new one.

The composite zone is CALM, with 41.9% of the 43 pairs diverging, 13 leaning bullish and 5 leaning bearish, for a net bias of -8. The mother jaws score is 100, so the calm average hides serious cracks in specific pairs.

The yield curve pair (t10y2y) moved from -0.60 to +0.35. Nvidia versus AMD moved from -0.91 to +0.30, and energy versus tech (xle_xlk) from -0.97 to -0.44.

VIX versus realized volatility moved from -0.54 to +0.06, which means implied and realized vol have stopped offsetting each other. Commodities versus the S&P 500 (dbc_spy) moved from -0.37 to +0.09.

Momentum versus the S&P 500 (mtum_spy) loosened from +0.84 to +0.44, so leadership is losing its grip on the index. Old relationships are breaking across rates, chips, energy and volatility at once, and that favors smaller positions and wider error bars.

AI read · what the confluences mean now

Two of three confluences are active today. T1 x HYG pairs volatility stress with credit stress, and T1 x JPY pairs it with yen safe-haven flow.

Credit weakness and yen demand are the two places where large money moves first when it wants out of risk. Both firing together says institutions are quietly de-risking while headline volatility stays contained.

The small-cap drawdown confluence (T1 x B2) is inactive, so the pain is not yet dragging the weakest part of the market into forced selling. Lean defensive: keep credit-sensitive and carry-trade exposure light, and use the yen and high-yield credit as your early read.

If the small-cap confluence lights up next, the move shifts from de-risking to liquidation.

Cross-Region Surveillance
Major indices from the 4 regions/asset classes. Asia trades ahead time-wise vs US — a Tokyo overnight crash often leaks into the SPX open. Crypto = 24h leading indicator of global risk appetite.
AI read · the cross-region tape

Every region closed the last five days lower except crypto, which is split. Asia is led by Shanghai (-2.5%) with Australia (^AXJO) the laggard at -5.8%.

Europe is led by Switzerland (-1.1%), the defensive market, while the Euro Stoxx 50 fell -3.7%. In the US, small caps (^RUT) lead at -5.1% and the Nasdaq 100 lags at -6.3%.

In crypto, Solana gained +4.3% while Bitcoin slipped -3.4%. The defensive leaders in Europe and the weak Nasdaq say money is leaving growth and tech first, and the global sell-off has no safe region.

Solana rising while Bitcoin falls shows speculative appetite in pockets, which fits a market searching for a bottom without finding one. For the US session, expect tech to stay under pressure unless the Nasdaq 100 stops lagging small caps.

A bounce in that gap would be the first sign sellers are tiring.

Forward-looking indicators · Bonferroni-validated
Crash Index — 10 lead-signal radar 6/10 · ALARM — 5+ signals aligned, action zone
AI read · volatility & crash, reconciled

The Crash Index at 6/10 and the VIX spike detector at tier 1/4 describe different layers of the same market. The Crash Index counts stress already visible in prices, breadth and credit, and five or more signals are aligned.

The VIX detector measures what the options market pays for protection, and it shows a 50% probability with skew active but no backwardation and no adaptive trigger. That is a coherent state: stocks have taken the hit, and traders have hedged through skew instead of buying front-month volatility.

Skew active means puts cost more than calls, so the fear is directional and targeted. The risk is that front-month protection is cheap relative to the stress in prices, which makes a sudden repricing sharp if the next leg down arrives.

Treat the Crash Index as the warning and the VIX tier as the trigger you are still waiting for.

Plain-English read · the Crash Index
Think of this as a smoke alarm, not a market forecast. Each of the 10 rows is a signal that led real crashes, checked over 15 years of S&P 500 history (Bonferroni-validated, so it survived a strict false-positive test). In a calm market it sits near zero by design — a low number is the alarm working, not a broken gauge. It only earns your attention when 3 or more rows light up together. Today it reads 6/10 — several signals are aligned, a real stress probability is building.

The stress (HYG/IEF, VIX3M/VIX, STLFSI4) ring at 5-30 days. The triggers (SPY -2% in 5d, VIX +30% in 3d) are short-term breakouts. For a tactical decision: 3+ signals simultaneously aligned = real probability of stress, never on isolated signal (framework rule).

Reading the table — Z-Score: number of standard deviations vs rolling 100d mean. |Z| > 2 = Kerberos entry threshold, |Z| > 2.5 = extreme (best R/R on mean-reversion). %B: position within Bollinger Bands (1.0 = upper band, 0 = lower band).

Aggregate reading — the mean of Z-scores gives a global regime indicator. Positive → cross-asset overbought market (Risk-On, watch reversal). Negative → oversold (Risk-Off, possible bottoming).
How to read
Persist = number of consecutive days above |Z| > 2.0 (Kerberos threshold). Persist ≥ 3d = validated signal (the divergence has become a regime, not a spike). Persist 1-2d = to watch. Persist 0d = dead signal. Sort on this column to find established regimes worth trading.
Glossary — 18 terms to understand the dashboard
Z-Score
Number of standard deviations vs the historical mean (rolling 100 days). Z=0 = normal level · |Z|>2 = stress · |Z|>2.5 = extreme.
Bollinger Bands
Bands drawn at ±2.2σ around a 100-day moving average. When the price exits the bands = statistically extreme signal.
Backwardation
Inverted curve: immediate fear exceeds far fear (e.g. VIX > VIX3M). Short-term panic signal.
Contango
Normal situation where far fear exceeds immediate fear. Extreme contango = complacency.
Half-life
Number of days required for a gap to the mean to halve. Measures the speed of mean-reversion.
Cointegration
Two assets that move together in the long term despite short-term fluctuations. Statistical basis of pair-trading.
Mean-reversion
Strategy betting that a gap to the mean will close. Inverse of momentum (which bets on continuation).
Breadth
Width of participation in the rally. Good breadth = many stocks rising. Bad breadth = only a few mega-caps pull the index.
Hedge ratio
Quantity of asset B to short to neutralize 1 long unit of asset A. Calculated via OLS regression on historical returns.
Lead-time
Delay between a signal's appearance and the event it predicts. Structural = 30-90d · stress = 5-30d · triggers = 1-10d.
Bonferroni
Statistical correction for multiple testing. When testing 100 signals, some seem valid by chance. Bonferroni divides the significance threshold by the number of tests to eliminate these false positives.
MCPT (Monte Carlo Permutation Test)
Robustness test: data is randomly shuffled 5000-10000 times to see if the signal appears by chance. If p < 0.05, the signal is probably real.
Walk-forward
Test where the model is trained on the first years (e.g. 2010-2020) and tested on the following years (2020-2025). Avoids in-sample overfitting.
Tail-hedge
Hedge against an extreme crash (-20% or more). Bought via deeply out-of-the-money puts. SKEW measures institutional demand for this type of insurance.
Mega-caps
The 7-10 largest market caps in the SPX (AAPL, MSFT, NVDA, GOOGL, AMZN, META, TSLA). Weigh ~35% of the index.
Cap-weighted vs Equal-weighted
SPY = weighted by capitalization (mega-caps dominate). RSP = each stock weighs 0.2%. Comparing both reveals concentration.
Risk parity
Portfolio strategy that balances risk (not capital) across asset classes. Stressed when stocks/bonds correlations turn positive (inflation regime).
framework rule
Fundamental principle: a solo signal = noise, 3+ aligned signals = real edge. All panel signals are Bonferroni-validated over 15 years of SPY.
